people.name: Adam Thierer
people.niche: free-market tech policy / permissionless innovation (R Street Institute)
people.reason: Leading libertarian voice on AI policy; has testified to Congress several times and argues in his own name for federal preemption of state AI laws, against ex-ante algorithmic audits, and against tort-heavy AI liability.

people.name: Neil Chilson
people.niche: free-market tech policy (Abundance Institute; former FTC chief technologist)
people.reason: Writes his own newsletter opposing state algorithmic-discrimination/audit bills, backing a national preemptive standard, and criticizing SB 53's whistleblower provisions.

people.name: Asad Ramzanali
people.niche: anti-monopoly tech policy (Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator; ex-OSTP)
people.reason: Signed op-ed in TIME explicitly calling to break up vertically integrated AI companies.
people.gap: antitrust-on-big-ai (hold side; statement had only one holder)

people.name: Matt Stoller
people.niche: anti-monopoly populism (American Economic Liberties Project, BIG newsletter)
people.reason: Prominent anti-monopolist who argues in his own newsletter for breaking up Google, including to stop it carrying its search monopoly into AI.

people.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
people.niche: Republican senator, Judiciary chair, longtime whistleblower advocate
people.reason: Introduced the AI Whistleblower Protection Act, with a statement in his own name.

works.author: sam-altman
works.title: Winning the AI Race: Strengthening U.S. Capabilities in Computing and Innovation (Senate Hearing 119-143)

statements.where: Altman's answer to Sen. Lummis on a 'patchwork' ('50 different sets of regulation', 'One Federal framework that is light touch'), and to Chairman Cruz on federal preemption ('one Federal approach ... sounds great to me')

works.note: Official hearing transcript with speaker labels; multi-witness, so the passage is attributed to 'Mr. Altman'. In the same hearing he answers Sen. Schatz that self-regulation is NOT enough ('some policy is good'), so don't tag him reject on binding-rules or profit-cannot-make-ai-safe from this work. Brad Smith and Michael Intrator say similar things about preemption here, but they are not on the map.

works.author: ted-cruz
works.title: Sen. Cruz Unveils AI Policy Framework to Strengthen American AI Leadership

statements.where: framework intro ('light-touch regulatory strategy'), the SANDBOX Act waiver description, and Cruz's quoted statement ('cut through bureaucratic red tape, and empower American AI developers')

works.note: A committee press release built around Cruz's signed statement and his own framework. The stance is a general light-touch / waiver position rather than a line that names frontier developers, so it is a moderate reject.

works.author: robin-hanson
works.title: AI Pause Regs Look Risky

statements.where: argues that regulating the few 'frontier AI firms' would have to expand without limit and need a world government; closes 'AI regs look bad by these two criteria'
middle paragraph: costs falling about 10x a year, so 'the number of nations, firms, and orgs who can afford to make, buy, or rent powerful AI is rising fast'

works.note: The binding-rules reject is clear. The concentrates-power reading is an aside about AI capability spreading, not a full argument about wealth and power, so treat it as weak.

works.author: adam-thierer
works.title: Testimony, Hearing on "AI at a Crossroads: A Nationwide Strategy or Californication?"

statements.where: 'a confusing patchwork of state and local legislative proposals'; recommendations: 'Congress should expressly preempt state regulations related to AI frontier labs and models'
second recommendation: 'Congress should preempt state efforts to preemptively regulate ... through cumbersome and confusing mechanisms such as AI audits or algorithmic impact assessments'

works.note: Do NOT tag binding-rules reject: in the same testimony he suggests NIST/CAISI oversee frontier model safety 'and Congress can give them additional authority'. On audits he rejects state ex-ante audits and allows that any ex-ante discrimination rules should be federal, so it is a reject of the mandate as framed, with that caveat.

works.author: adam-thierer
works.title: America's Litigation Addiction Threatens Its AI Leadership

statements.where: opening section: the suits by parents of teens against AI companies rest 'on a fundamental misunderstanding'; 'if state lawmakers proposing new AI liability schemes have their way'; praises Section 230's 'liability shield' as the model

works.note: Sole byline Adam Thierer (R Street author link). It argues against expanding tort liability for AI makers, not against all liability, so it is a reject of the liability push rather than of any accountability at all.

works.author: neil-chilson
works.title: Red Flags in AI Legislation

statements.where: urges Youngkin to veto Virginia's bill; the database analogy ('file reports and audits to ensure that the database was unbiased'); calls state AI rules 'the Red Flag Laws of the 21st century'

works.note: Byline 'Neil' on his own newsletter (Neil Chilson). Aimed at Colorado-style algorithmic-discrimination laws for consequential decisions, which is the statement's subject.

works.author: neil-chilson
works.title: Raising the Cost of Bad AI Laws

statements.where: his commentary on the preemption executive order: a 'stopgap against the worst state AI laws until Congress does the necessary work of establishing a minimally burdensome national standard'; calls the DOJ task force for suing states 'based'

works.note: Supports a national standard displacing state AI laws, and also notes that the EO itself creates no new preemption.

works.author: neil-chilson
works.title: More on SB 53

statements.where: section 'SB 53's whistleblower provisions have serious side-effects' (calls it a 'Can't Fire AI Doomers Act', a 'de facto layoff shield', a 'discovery goldmine')

works.note: QUALIFIED: his conclusion says 'Keep whistleblower protections, but calibrate' them. Readers may score this as neutral or a conditional hold. It is the closest thing to a reject that I found; no figure I checked rejects AI whistleblower protection outright.

works.author: dean-ball
works.title: The AI Patchwork Emerges

statements.where: 'I have long been a supporter of a federal AI law with broad (though not universal) preemption of state regulations'; says his proposal would preempt 'almost literally every law I have described'

works.note: Ball holds binding-rules-for-frontier-ai on the map, and this does not conflict: he wants federal rules that preempt the states. He also restates opposition to algorithmic-discrimination laws here, but he is already a reject on ai-bias-audits-required.

works.author: noah-smith
works.title: What the AI boom is doing for Americans

statements.where: rebuttal of Krugman's 'technology of, by and for oligarchs': 'I think that this is basically wrong', then benefits flowing to regular Americans (jobs, fiscal, consumer)

works.note: MODERATE: he argues that the gains are spread widely, which is the reject side, but he also says Americans 'could stand to benefit more'. It is about who gets the benefits, not explicitly about corporate power.

works.author: noah-smith
works.title: I'm kind of over the whole "Anti-monopoly" movement

statements.where: early paragraph recapping his Bloomberg years: 'Big Tech companies were a bad target for antitrust enforcement'; the rest of the piece criticizes the antimonopoly movement

works.note: The key line is a parenthetical recap of his earlier view, and the piece is not AI-specific. The reject is clear but short.

works.author: mark-zuckerberg
works.title: Mark Zuckerberg's internal Q&A, full transcript (published by The Verge)
works.channel: The Verge (leaked internal meeting audio, full transcript)

statements.where: section 'On the potential breakup of Facebook': 'breaking up these companies, whether it's Facebook or Google or Amazon, is not actually going to solve the issues'; 'you go to the mat and you fight'

works.note: Verbatim speaker-labelled transcript of internal employee meetings, published by The Verge. The words are his own, but they were not meant for the public. Pre-AI-boom (2019), but about the largest tech companies. Benjamin may want to rule on whether leaked internal remarks count.

works.author: asad-ramzanali
works.title: Break Up Big AI Before It Breaks Us

statements.where: 'The first step to a healthier market is to break up companies that are vertically integrated'; 'Chips must be independent from clouds, and clouds must be independent from AI models'; closing line

works.note: time.com returns 406 to curl, but WebFetch loaded the full text and confirmed the byline and passages.

works.author: matt-stoller
works.title: The Proposal to Break Up Google Is Finally Here

statements.where: his defence of the DOJ remedy (Chrome divestiture) to stop Google leveraging search 'to control future markets, most notably artificial intelligence-based search models'; 'lawbreakers don't get to enjoy the fruits'

works.note: Free post. He endorses the breakup remedy for Google. It is a specific company and case, not a general call for every AI firm.

works.author: chuck-grassley
works.title: Grassley Introduces AI Whistleblower Protection Act

statements.where: Grassley's quoted statement: 'too many people working in AI feel they're unable to speak up ... We need to act to make these protections crystal clear ... protect AI whistleblowers'

works.note: The bill protects disclosures to federal agencies and Congress, not to the general public; the statement says 'warn the public', which is a slight mismatch. The release also quotes co-sponsors Coons, Schatz and Obernolte, and lists on-map senators Blackburn and Hawley as co-sponsors without quoting them, so it is not their work.

summary.note: Web search budget ran out partway through. The rest of the work used direct fetches of authors' own sites and Substack archive APIs, so coverage is thinner than intended. JD Vance's Paris speech (presidency.ucsb.edu) was a strong binding-rules reject, but it is already in seed, so it was dropped.
